_metadata.disclaimer: This system provides guided first-aid instructions based on verified medical protocols. It does not replace professional medical care. Always call emergency services immediately. All protocols are rule-based and medically reviewed. No LLM or AI inference is used for treatment decisions.

triage_priority_system.description: Rule-based priority engine. Evaluates selected conditions and assigns response priority. Based on ABCDE framework (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure).

P1_IMMEDIATE.label: IMMEDIATE - Life Threatening
P1_IMMEDIATE.description: Conditions that will cause death within minutes without intervention.

P2_URGENT.label: URGENT - Serious
P2_URGENT.description: Serious conditions that can deteriorate rapidly but allow a brief window for action.

P3_DELAYED.label: DELAYED - Moderate
P3_DELAYED.description: Injuries that are serious but stable. Victim is conscious and able to communicate.

P4_MINIMAL.label: MINIMAL - Walking Wounded
P4_MINIMAL.description: Minor injuries. Victim is ambulatory and able to follow instructions.

questions.question: Is the victim speaking or making sounds?
Can you see any visible obstruction in the mouth?
Check chest rise — is it equal on both sides?
Check the victim's skin color and feel
What is the victim's level of consciousness? (AVPU Scale)
Can the victim move their limbs?
Check pupils — are they equal and reactive?
Any additional injuries found on body check?

priority_matrix.description: Rule engine: maps condition combinations to protocol sequence. Evaluated in order. First match wins unless multi-condition override applies.

rules.reasoning: Cardiac/respiratory arrest — highest priority. CPR doubles survival chance. AHA 2025.
Cardiac arrest. Begin compressions immediately. AHA 2025.
Exsanguination risk. Apply direct pressure + tourniquet if limb. AHA 2024.
Multi-life-threat. Control catastrophic bleeding before CPR. TCCC + AHA.
Do not move. 40% spinal injuries from MVA. AHA/ERC 2025.
Unconscious but breathing — recovery position prevents aspiration. ERC 2025.
Spinal injury + unconscious — modified handling required. ERC 2025.
Complete airway obstruction — Heimlich maneuver. AHA 2024.
Tension pneumothorax risk. 3-sided occlusive dressing. AHA 2024.
Major burns >10% — cool, cover, treat shock. GRSP & AHA.
Protect from injury. Do not restrain. AHA 2024.
Circulatory shock — lay flat, elevate legs if no spinal, keep warm. AHA 2024.
Do not release crush suddenly — rhabdomyolysis risk. AHA 2024.
Head injury assumes spinal risk. Immobilize. AHA/ERC 2025.
NEVER remove impaled objects. Stabilize in place. AHA 2024.

PROTO_SCENE_SAFETY.name: Scene Safety Check
PROTO_SCENE_SAFETY.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024, GRSP Road Crash First Response

steps.detail: Look for ongoing traffic, fire, fuel leaks, unstable vehicles, or electrical hazards before approaching.
Turn on hazard lights. Place warning triangles 50m behind the vehicle. Signal other drivers to slow down.
Call 112 (or 108 in India) immediately. State location, number of victims, and injuries visible.
If available, put on disposable gloves before touching the victim to prevent disease transmission.
Approach the victim from a direction that does not expose you to hazards. Do not move victim unless in immediate danger.

do_not: Do NOT approach if the scene is actively unsafe (fire, moving traffic, live electricity).
Do NOT move a victim from a vehicle unless there is fire or immediate life threat.
Do NOT turn off a victim's vehicle ignition if it is the only source of stability.

PROTO_CPR.name: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) - Adult
PROTO_CPR.source: AHA CPR Guidelines 2025 | AHA & Red Cross 2024 First Aid Guidelines | ERC 2025

steps.detail: Tap shoulders firmly and shout 'Are you OK?' If no response, confirm not breathing normally (gasping does NOT count as breathing). Check for no more than 10 seconds.
Shout for help. Ask bystander to call 112/108. Ask another to find an AED if available. If alone, call first then begin CPR.
Place victim on their back on a firm, flat surface. Kneel beside their chest.
Place heel of one hand on the CENTER of the chest on the lower half of the sternum (breastbone). Place other hand on top. Interlace fingers and keep them off the ribs.

Push STRAIGHT DOWN. Rate: 100-120 compressions per minute (rhythm of 'Stayin' Alive'). Depth: at least 2 inches (5cm), not more than 2.4 inches (6cm). Allow FULL chest recoil between each compression. Keep your shoulders directly over hands and elbows locked.

After 30 compressions: tilt head back, lift chin. Pinch nose shut. Take a normal breath. Make complete seal over mouth. Give 1 breath over 1 second — watch chest rise. Give second breath. Total pause should be under 10 seconds. Ratio: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
steps.untrained_alternative: Hands-only CPR: continuous compressions without breaths is acceptable for untrained rescuers.

steps.detail: Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths. Switch rescuers every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue. Do NOT stop until: AED is available, professional help takes over, victim starts breathing normally, or you are physically unable to continue.

steps.action: Apply AED as soon as available
steps.detail: Turn AED on. Attach pads to bare dry chest as shown on pads. Follow AED voice instructions. Clear all persons before shock. Resume compressions immediately after shock.

do_not: Do NOT stop CPR to check for pulse — this wastes critical time.
Do NOT lean on chest between compressions — full recoil is essential.
Do NOT give aggressive or rapid ventilation — 1 breath over 1 second only.
Do NOT compress faster than 120/min — shallow compressions result.
Do NOT compress deeper than 6cm — can cause internal injury.
Do NOT give water or anything by mouth to an unconscious person.
Survival decreases 7-10% per minute without CPR — start immediately.
PROTO_CPR.survival_note: Immediate CPR doubles or triples survival chance after cardiac arrest. ERC 2025 — 'Start CPR without worrying about accidentally hurting the person. It is more important to try to save their life.'

PROTO_BLEEDING_SEVERE.name: Severe / Life-Threatening Bleeding Control
PROTO_BLEEDING_SEVERE.source: AHA & Red Cross First Aid Guidelines 2024 | Stop The Bleed Program | ERC 2025

steps.detail: Put on gloves if available before touching blood.
Press a clean cloth, clothing, or bandage FIRMLY over the wound. Apply continuous strong pressure with both hands. Do NOT remove cloth if soaked — add more on top.

If the wound is on an arm or leg AND direct pressure is not stopping bleeding: apply a tourniquet 5-8cm (2-3 inches) above the wound. Tighten until bleeding stops. Note the time applied. Commercial tourniquet is ideal; improvised tourniquet using belt or cloth is acceptable.
For wounds in groin, armpit, or neck where tourniquet cannot be applied: pack wound tightly with cloth or gauze. Apply firm pressure over packed wound continuously.
Raise the injured arm or leg above heart level IF no fracture is suspected. This slows blood loss.
Keep victim still and calm. Monitor for signs of shock (pale, cold, rapid breathing, confusion). Maintain pressure until professional help arrives.

do_not: Do NOT remove embedded objects or impaled items from a wound — this can cause rapid fatal bleeding.
Do NOT remove tourniquet once applied — only trained professionals should remove it.
Do NOT apply tourniquet directly over a joint.
Do NOT give water or food to victim.
Do NOT use a tourniquet on the neck, chest, or abdomen.

PROTO_BLEEDING_MODERATE.name: Moderate Bleeding Control

steps.detail: Press clean cloth firmly over the wound. Hold for at least 5 minutes without lifting. If soaked, add more cloth on top.
Raise injured limb above heart level if no fracture is suspected.
Once bleeding slows, secure cloth with bandage or tape. Do not remove.
Watch for increasing blood loss or signs of shock. Keep victim calm and still.

do_not: Do NOT lift cloth to check wound — this breaks forming clot.
Do NOT apply a tourniquet unless bleeding is life-threatening.

PROTO_RECOVERY_POSITION.name: Recovery Position — Unconscious Breathing Victim
PROTO_RECOVERY_POSITION.source: ERC 2025 | AHA & Red Cross 2024 | ILCOR 2022 Systematic Review
PROTO_RECOVERY_POSITION.note: Do NOT use if spinal injury, hip/pelvis injury, or if CPR may be needed.

steps.detail: Position yourself on one side of the victim who is lying on their back.
Place the arm closest to you at a right angle to the body, elbow bent with palm facing up.
Bring the victim's far arm across their chest and hold the back of their hand against their nearest cheek.
Lift the victim's far knee so the foot is flat on the ground.
Pull the bent knee toward you, rolling the victim onto their side. Support head to keep airway open.
Tilt head back gently and open mouth slightly to allow drainage. Ensure airway is clear.
Check breathing every minute. If breathing stops — begin CPR immediately.

do_not: Do NOT use recovery position if spinal injury is suspected — use log-roll only with trained rescuers.
Do NOT leave victim alone.
Do NOT give anything by mouth.

PROTO_SPINAL_INJURY.name: Suspected Spinal Injury Management
PROTO_SPINAL_INJURY.source: ERC 2025 | AHA & Red Cross 2024 | ILCOR Scoping Review 2024 | ATLS 10th Ed.
PROTO_SPINAL_INJURY.note: Motor vehicle crashes cause 40% of spinal cord injuries. High suspicion in ALL road crash victims. ILCOR 2024: Cervical collars are NOT recommended for lay first aiders as they may impair respiration and raise intracranial pressure.

steps.detail: Calmly instruct the victim to stay completely still. Do NOT move their head or neck.
Only if absolutely necessary, hold head gently in the position you found it — do NOT straighten or turn the neck. Use both hands to support the head from the sides without pressing.
Do NOT move victim to a more comfortable position. Keep them where they are unless there is immediate life danger (fire, water, collapsing structure).
Watch for breathing difficulty. If victim stops breathing and CPR is required — airway takes priority over spinal precautions. Begin CPR and open airway.
Keep victim calm and warm. Talk to them continuously. Wait for professional help.

do_not: Do NOT move the victim unless in immediate life danger.
Do NOT twist, bend, or straighten the neck.
Do NOT remove a motorcycle or bicycle helmet unless victim cannot breathe.
Do NOT apply a cervical collar unless professionally trained — ILCOR 2024 advises against lay use.
Do NOT leave victim alone.

PROTO_AIRWAY_MANAGEMENT.name: Airway Opening — Conscious Victim

steps.detail: Help victim sit upright or lean forward slightly. This helps open airway. Do NOT do this if spinal injury suspected.
If no spinal injury suspected: gently tilt head back by placing one hand on forehead, two fingers of other hand under chin to lift it upward.
Place fingers behind angle of jaw on both sides. Push jaw forward without moving neck.
If foreign material is clearly visible in mouth, carefully remove with fingers. Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps.
Watch for chest rise, listen for breath sounds, feel for air. If breathing stops, begin CPR immediately.

do_not: Do NOT perform blind finger sweeps — can push obstruction deeper.
Do NOT tilt head if spinal injury suspected.
Do NOT give water to victim with breathing difficulty.

PROTO_CHOKING.name: Choking — Airway Obstruction

steps.detail: If victim can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing. Do NOT interfere.
Stand to the side and slightly behind. Support chest with one hand. Give 5 firm blows between shoulder blades with heel of other hand.

Stand behind victim. Wrap arms around waist. Make fist with one hand, place thumb side against abdomen just above navel and below breastbone. Grasp fist with other hand. Give 5 firm upward and inward thrusts.
Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until object is expelled or victim becomes unconscious.
Lower victim to ground carefully. Call emergency services if not done. Begin CPR — chest compressions can help dislodge obstruction. Look in mouth before rescue breaths.

modifications.pregnant_or_obese: Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts. Place hands at lower breastbone.
modifications.infant_under_1_year: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts (NOT abdominal thrusts). Support head.

do_not: Do NOT perform abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year.
Do NOT do blind finger sweeps.
Do NOT hold victim upside down.

PROTO_OPEN_CHEST.name: Open Chest Wound (Sucking Chest Wound)
PROTO_OPEN_CHEST.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 | TCCC Guidelines | ATLS 10th Ed.

steps.detail: Apply an occlusive (airtight) dressing over the wound. Use commercial vented chest seal if available. If not: use plastic wrap, credit card, or any airtight material. Tape 3 sides only (leave one side open as a flutter valve to allow air to escape).
Position sitting upright or inclined on the injured side if breathing is easier. Do NOT lay flat unless spinal injury is ruled out and airway is at risk.
Watch for increased difficulty breathing, which may indicate tension pneumothorax. If dressing appears to be blocking air escape, briefly lift corner to burp.
This is a critical injury. Requires hospital intervention urgently.

do_not: Do NOT remove any object from the chest.
Do NOT seal all four sides — tension pneumothorax risk.
Do NOT lay flat if breathing is very difficult.

PROTO_HEAD_INJURY.name: Head Injury Management
PROTO_HEAD_INJURY.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 | ATLS 10th Ed. | NICE Head Injury Guidelines

steps.detail: Assume spinal injury with any head injury. Do NOT move head or neck. Activate PROTO_SPINAL_INJURY alongside.
Scalp wounds bleed heavily. Apply firm gentle pressure with clean cloth. Do NOT apply pressure over suspected skull fracture — apply pressure around the wound.
Talk to victim continuously. Check AVPU every 2 minutes. Any deterioration is serious. Note: confusion, vomiting, unequal pupils, fluid from ears/nose are all danger signs.
If victim vomits: turn head to side using log-roll technique to clear airway, maintaining spinal precautions.
No aspirin, ibuprofen, or pain killers. These can worsen brain or bleeding complications.

danger_signs: Fluid from ears or nose (possible skull fracture / CSF leak)
Worsening confusion or loss of consciousness
do_not: Do NOT leave unconscious head injury victim lying face up without monitoring airway.
Do NOT remove objects embedded in skull.
Do NOT give aspirin or ibuprofen.
Do NOT apply pressure directly over suspected skull fracture.
Do NOT move victim without spinal precautions.

PROTO_SHOCK.name: Shock Management
PROTO_SHOCK.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 | ATLS 10th Ed. | ERC 2025

steps.detail: Shock is life threatening. Call 112/108 immediately if not done.
Help victim lie on back on a flat surface. Do NOT do this if: spinal injury suspected, unconscious (use recovery position), or breathing is worse when flat.
Raise legs 20-30cm (about 12 inches) above heart level. Do NOT elevate if: fracture of legs/pelvis, spinal injury, or head injury. This helps blood flow to vital organs.
Identify and control any source of bleeding. Shock is often caused by blood loss.
Cover with blanket or clothing. Prevent heat loss. Do NOT overheat.
Speak calmly. Tell victim help is coming. Anxiety worsens shock.
Check breathing, pulse, and consciousness every 2 minutes.

do_not: Do NOT give water, food, or anything by mouth — surgery may be needed.
Do NOT allow victim to stand or walk.
Do NOT leave victim alone.
Do NOT apply heating pad or hot water bottles — can cause burns.
Do NOT elevate legs if head/spine/pelvis injury is suspected.

PROTO_BURN_MAJOR.name: Major Burns (>10% Body Surface Area)
PROTO_BURN_MAJOR.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 | GRSP Road Crash First Response | ATLS

steps.detail: Ensure victim is away from fire, heat, or chemical source. Protect yourself from same hazard.
Remove clothing from burned areas UNLESS it is stuck to the burn. Remove rings, watches, belts before swelling begins.
Immediately run cool (NOT ice cold) running water over the burn for a minimum of 20 minutes. This is the most important step. Do NOT use ice, butter, toothpaste, oil, or any cream.
After cooling, cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy material. Cling film (plastic wrap) is ideal. Do NOT use cotton wool or fluffy materials that can stick.
Major burns cause severe fluid loss and shock. Keep victim warm. Do NOT give water if victim may need surgery.
Burns to face/mouth may cause airway swelling. Watch for increasing voice changes, stridor, or difficulty breathing. Airway burns are immediately life threatening.

do_not: Do NOT use ice or ice-cold water — can cause frostbite and worsen shock.
Do NOT apply butter, oil, toothpaste, or any home remedies.
Do NOT break blisters.
Do NOT remove clothing stuck to the burn.
Do NOT wrap tightly — burned areas swell significantly.
Do NOT give food or water if major burn — surgery likely needed.

PROTO_BURN_MINOR.name: Minor Burns (Small Area, 1st or 2nd Degree)

steps.detail: Run cool water over burn for at least 10-20 minutes.
Apply a non-adhesive clean dressing. Do NOT wrap tightly.
Seek medical care if burn covers more than palm size, is on face/hands/feet/genitals, or blisters form.

do_not: Do NOT use ice.
Do NOT burst blisters.
Do NOT apply any cream or home remedy before cooling.

PROTO_BURN_CHEMICAL.name: Chemical Burn

steps.detail: Do NOT touch chemical with bare hands. Wear gloves if available.
If chemical is dry/powder, brush off with cloth BEFORE washing. Do NOT add water to dry chemicals first — this can activate them.

steps.action: Flush with large amounts of water
steps.detail: Run large amounts of water over the affected area for 20-30 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing while flushing.
Cover loosely. All chemical burns require hospital assessment.

do_not: Do NOT use neutralizing agents — can cause heat reaction.
Do NOT rub chemical into skin.

PROTO_BURN_ELECTRICAL.name: Electrical Burn / Electrocution

steps.action: Do NOT touch victim while in contact with electricity
steps.detail: Turn off power source first. If not possible, use non-conductive material (wood, plastic, rubber) to move victim away. Never use metal.
Electrical injuries frequently cause cardiac arrest. Immediately check for breathing and pulse.
Cool visible burns with water. Note there may be entry AND exit wounds.
steps.note: Internal damage often far greater than visible surface burn

steps.detail: All electrical injuries require hospital evaluation regardless of visible burn size — internal damage may not be apparent.

do_not: Do NOT touch victim while still in contact with electricity.
Do NOT assume victim is fine because external burn is small.

PROTO_FRACTURE_CLOSED.name: Closed Fracture (Bone Not Visible)

steps.action: Do not move victim if back/neck/pelvis fracture suspected
steps.detail: Treat breathing, bleeding, and shock first before addressing fractures.
Support the injured limb in the position you found it. Do NOT try to straighten or realign. Use padding, rolled clothing, or improvised splint to support.

steps.action: Splint — immobilize joint above and below fracture
steps.detail: If splinting: place padding around limb. Splint must extend beyond the joint above and below the fracture. Bind loosely — not so tight as to cut circulation.
Check fingers/toes below fracture site — they should be warm and pink. If blue, cold, or numb: splint may be too tight — loosen immediately.
Gently elevate immobilized limb to reduce swelling if movement does not cause pain.

do_not: Do NOT attempt to straighten or reset a fracture.
Do NOT apply pressure to the fracture site.
Do NOT move victim if spine/pelvis fracture suspected.
Do NOT give food or water if surgery may be needed.
Do NOT remove shoes/socks unless circulation is compromised.

PROTO_FRACTURE_OPEN.name: Open Fracture (Bone Visible Through Skin)

steps.detail: Apply gentle pressure around (NOT over) the exposed bone. Use clean cloth or dressing.
Cover exposed bone and wound with clean moist dressing. Do NOT push bone back in.
Immobilize limb in position found. Do NOT try to realign.
Open fractures bleed significantly. Watch for shock signs.

do_not: Do NOT push bone back into wound.
Do NOT clean the wound.
Do NOT apply tourniquet unless life-threatening hemorrhage.

PROTO_SEIZURE.name: Seizure / Convulsions Management

steps.detail: Clear the area of hard or sharp objects. Cushion head with soft material (jacket, bag). Time the seizure from onset.
Do NOT hold victim down or try to stop convulsions. This can cause injury.
Gently turn victim to their side once convulsions ease to prevent choking on fluids. Maintain this position.
Note seizure duration. Most stop within 1-3 minutes. After seizure: victim may be confused — this is normal. Keep calm, protect airway.
Call immediately if: seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, victim does not regain consciousness, second seizure follows, victim is injured, victim is pregnant, or this is their first known seizure.

do_not: Do NOT put anything in mouth during seizure.
Do NOT hold victim down.
Do NOT give water until fully conscious.
Do NOT restrain convulsing limbs.

PROTO_CHEST_PAIN.name: Chest Pain (Suspected Heart Attack)
PROTO_CHEST_PAIN.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 — 'In adults with acute chest pain, activate EMS to initiate transport to closest ED.'

steps.detail: Chest pain in adults is a medical emergency. Call 112/108 immediately. Every minute matters.
Have victim sit or lie in the most comfortable position — often sitting upright with knees bent. Do NOT allow them to walk around.
Loosen collar, tie, belt, or anything tight around chest or neck.

steps.action: Aspirin if available and not allergic
steps.detail: If victim is conscious, has no allergy to aspirin, is not on blood thinners, and can swallow: give 300mg aspirin (adult full tablet) to chew slowly. Do NOT give if victim has internal bleeding.
Watch for loss of consciousness. If victim stops breathing — begin CPR immediately.

warning_signs: Pain radiating to arm (left), jaw, neck, or back
do_not: Do NOT allow victim to drive themselves.
Do NOT leave victim alone.
Do NOT give aspirin if allergic or unconscious.
Do NOT give food or water.

PROTO_CRUSH_INJURY.name: Crush Injury / Trapped Body Part
PROTO_CRUSH_INJURY.source: AHA & Red Cross 2024 | ATLS | Rhabdomyolysis Medical Guidelines

steps.detail: Crush injuries require specialized rescue. Call 112/108 immediately.
Sudden release after prolonged crush causes deadly 'crush syndrome' — toxic release from damaged muscle into bloodstream. Only trained rescuers should manage release after >15 minutes of entrapment.
Apply pressure to any visible bleeding wounds around the trapped area.
Crush victims develop shock rapidly. Monitor breathing, pulse, consciousness.
Prevent hypothermia. Talk continuously. Professional rescue equipment required.

do_not: Do NOT rapidly release a victim trapped for more than 15 minutes — fatal cardiac arrest risk.
Do NOT apply tourniquets above trapped limb unless life-threatening bleed.
Do NOT give water — kidney failure risk after crush.

PROTO_IMPALED_OBJECT.name: Embedded / Impaled Object in Body

steps.detail: The impaled object may be plugging a major blood vessel. Removing it can cause fatal hemorrhage.
Build up padding around the object (rolled cloth, bandages) to prevent it from moving. Secure lightly.
Apply pressure to bleeding around the object — NOT to the object itself.
Keep victim as still as possible to prevent object from shifting.
Object removal must be done in a hospital operating environment.

do_not: Do NOT remove impaled object under any circumstances.
Do NOT shorten the object unless essential for rescue.
Do NOT press on the object.

PROTO_SPINAL_CPR_CONFLICT.name: Spinal Injury + Unconscious — Conflict Protocol
PROTO_SPINAL_CPR_CONFLICT.source: ERC 2025 | AHA 2025 — Airway takes priority over spinal precautions when life is at immediate risk.
PROTO_SPINAL_CPR_CONFLICT.rule: AIRWAY AND BREATHING ARE ALWAYS PRIORITY ONE. Spinal precautions are secondary when victim is in cardiac/respiratory arrest.

steps.detail: Is victim breathing? If YES and unconscious — use gentle log-roll to recovery position with minimal neck movement.
Open airway using jaw thrust (preferred with suspected spinal injury). If jaw thrust fails to open airway, use head-tilt chin-lift — saving life takes priority over spinal precautions.
Keep head as neutral as possible during compressions. Use jaw thrust for breaths. One rescuer can stabilize head while another compresses if multiple rescuers present.

PROTO_SYNCOPE.name: Fainting / Syncope

steps.detail: If victim faints or feels faint, lower to ground or flat surface immediately to prevent injury from fall.
Raise legs 30cm above heart level. This increases blood flow to brain.
Loosen any tight clothing around neck or chest.
Most people regain consciousness within 1 minute. Do NOT sit them up immediately — wait until fully recovered.
Call 112 if: no recovery within 1 minute, chest pain, head injury from fall, pregnant, diabetic, or first time fainting with no known cause.

do_not: Do NOT give water until fully conscious.
Do NOT hold smelling salts near victim.
Do NOT sit victim up immediately after regaining consciousness.

steps.detail: If victim is vomiting, immediately turn to their side to allow vomit to drain and prevent choking.
After episode, check mouth and clear any visible obstruction. Do NOT perform blind finger sweep.
Do not give water or fluids if victim may have internal injury or need surgery.
Listen for gurgling breathing. If gurgling — airway obstruction from vomit. Position, open airway, call emergency.

PROTO_EYE_INJURY.name: Eye Injury

steps.detail: Rubbing can worsen injury or embed objects deeper.

steps.action: Flush with clean water for chemical exposure
steps.detail: If chemical — flush immediately with clean water for 15-20 minutes.
Cover both eyes loosely (not tightly) with a clean cloth. Covering both reduces eye movement.
If object is embedded in eye — do NOT remove. Stabilize around it and seek immediate care.

do_not: Do NOT rub eye.
Do NOT remove embedded objects.
Do NOT apply pressure to eyeball.

PROTO_ABDOMINAL_INJURY.name: Abdominal Injury

steps.action: Lay victim flat with knees bent
steps.detail: Help victim lie on back with knees slightly bent to relax abdominal muscles. If eviscerating wound (organs visible) — do NOT push back, cover with moist clean cloth.

steps.action: Do NOT give food or water
steps.detail: Abdominal injuries almost always require surgery.
Abdominal injuries cause significant internal bleeding.
All significant abdominal trauma requires hospital evaluation.

do_not: Do NOT give food or water.
Do NOT push exposed organs back.
Do NOT remove impaled objects.

PROTO_DIABETIC.name: Diabetic Emergency (Hypoglycemia Suspected)

steps.detail: Confusion, sweating, trembling, pale, rapid pulse, slurred speech, weakness — in a known diabetic victim.

steps.action: Give sugar if conscious and able to swallow
steps.detail: Give glucose gel, sugar dissolved in water, fruit juice, or candy. Victim must be conscious and able to swallow safely.
Most improve within 10-15 minutes. Repeat sugar if no improvement in 10 minutes.
Call 112 if: victim is unconscious, no improvement after 10-15 minutes, seizure occurs.

do_not: Do NOT give sugar to an unconscious victim — aspiration risk.
Do NOT delay giving sugar to a conscious diabetic victim.

key_voice_cues.text_en: Start chest compressions now. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest.
Push at 100 to 120 times per minute. Follow the beeping rhythm.
Give two rescue breaths now. Tilt head, pinch nose, breathe in for one second.
Continue CPR. Do not stop. Professional help is on the way.
Apply firm pressure to the wound with a cloth. Press hard and do not lift.
Roll the victim gently onto their side. Keep airway open. Watch for breathing.
Suspected spine injury. Do not move the victim. Keep them still and calm.
Do not restrain the victim. Clear the area. Protect the head. Time the seizure.
Emergency services have been notified. Stay on the line and follow instructions.
